strengths: Large-scale synthetic HDR dataset (24,000 images) addresses a critical bottleneck—~200x larger than existing datasets, solving the limited real-world data problem
Well-designed rendering pipeline with thoughtful technical choices (linear color space, floating-point storage, camera shake simulation) demonstrating engineering quality
Comprehensive experimental validation including ablation studies, cross-dataset generalization tests, and evaluation on both labeled/unlabeled data with multiple metrics (PSNR, SSIM, HDR-VDP2)
Consistent and significant improvements demonstrated across multiple architectures and test sets (e.g., 2dB gain on Challenge123 PSNR-µ), with strong visual results showing artifact reduction
Thorough dataset analysis with quantitative diversity metrics and t-SNE visualization demonstrating superior coverage compared to existing datasets
Practical, plug-and-play domain adaptation method that works across CNN and Transformer architectures with zero inference overhead via re-parameterization
Strong reproducibility with detailed implementation details, appendices, and promised code/dataset release
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: adapter design closely follows VIDA [24] and LoRA [14] without substantial HDR-specific adaptations; test-time adaptation uses standard mean-teacher framework; uncertainty-based scale adjustment (Eq. 2) is overly simplistic without principled justification
Significant domain gap remains (Figs. 2, A1) in texture-rich regions despite sophisticated rendering; insufficient analysis of gap causes or solutions to address remaining mismatches
Missing critical ablations: no data scaling study to isolate quality vs. quantity benefits; no ablation on rendering parameters; no analysis of which scenarios contribute most to improvement

Insufficient statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing; marginal improvements on some metrics (SSIM <0.002); very small test sets (27-36 samples) raise generalization concerns
No comparison with alternative domain adaptation methods—only compares against baselines trained on real data, not other adaptation strategies, preventing assessment of adapter optimality
Hyperparameter choices lack justification: rank values (rs=1, rt=64) and augmentation parameters borrowed without HDR-specific validation; no sensitivity analysis provided

Rendering validation gaps: no quantitative comparison of rendered vs. real sensor characteristics; limited analysis of camera shake effectiveness; unclear if rendering detail matches actual camera properties
Computational overhead of test-time adaptation not analyzed; requires N forward passes but inference cost not reported despite practical deployment concerns
Limited evaluation scope: only two small real-world test datasets; no evaluation on diverse camera sensors or extreme scenarios; unclear generalization to other HDR applications
Evaluation limited to two datasets with significant domain-specific characteristics; lacks broader real-world validation beyond SCT and Challenge123

strengths: Large-scale, high-quality synthetic HDR dataset (24,000 images) that substantially exceeds prior work and addresses a real bottleneck in the field
Thoughtfully designed rendering pipeline with careful attention to realistic synthesis, including tone mapping, camera shake, and multiple auxiliary outputs
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with extensive ablations, multiple datasets, multiple metrics, and both supervised and unsupervised adaptation scenarios
Strong empirical improvements on synthetic benchmarks (6+ dB on SCT) demonstrating dataset effectiveness
Clear presentation with good visualizations of dataset diversity and domain gap analysis
Full reproducibility with publicly available code and dataset
Solid technical execution and proper experimental methodology throughout
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty - S2R-Adapter applies straightforward existing adapter designs (shared/transfer branches) without significant innovation
Modest improvements on real-world datasets (0.4-0.6 dB on Challenge123), contradicting claims of 'state-of-the-art' performance and suggesting the domain gap problem is not fully solved
Weak evidence for domain adaptation effectiveness - t-SNE visualizations show visible cluster separation, indicating the shared branch may not fully capture domain-invariant features
Insufficient analysis of what dataset characteristics drive improvements - lacks deeper insight beyond 'larger scale and more diversity'
Uncertainty-based scale factor adjustment (Eq. 2) appears ad-hoc and lacks thorough justification or validation of the specific formulation
Test-time adaptation adds 0.23 seconds per image overhead, limiting practical applicability for video/batch processing
Limited comparison with alternative domain adaptation methods - primarily compares against simple fine-tuning rather than other domain adaptation strategies
No ablation or justification for key design choices (e.g., low-rank vs. full-rank projections, specific rank selections)
Lacks analysis of failure cases and limitations of the proposed approach
Camera motion synthesis validation missing - synthesized Perlin noise motion distributions not validated against real-world characteristics

strengths: Addresses a critical and practical need in HDR fusion research by providing the first large-scale (24,000 images) high-quality synthetic HDR dataset with comprehensive diversity in scenes, lighting conditions, and motion types
Sophisticated rendering pipeline using Unreal Engine 5 with proper tone mapping, gamma correction, and precise control over environmental factors, producing realistic HDR images suitable for training

Well-designed domain adaptation method (S2R-Adapter) that effectively bridges the synthetic-to-real gap through a principled two-branch architecture (shared and transfer branches) with uncertainty-aware scaling

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (SCT, Challenge123, Kalantiarn, Sen's, Tursun's) with consistent improvements (0.6dB on SCT, 2dB on Challenge123) and ablation studies validating each component
Excellent reproducibility with detailed implementation descriptions, promised code/dataset release, multiple evaluation metrics, and clear methodology suitable for community use

Strong generalization results showing that models trained on S2R-HDR outperform those trained on smaller real-world datasets, with clear visual improvements in artifact reduction and highlight recovery
High-quality presentation with clear motivation, excellent visualizations demonstrating both quantitative improvements and qualitative visual quality gains
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty - the two-branch adapter uses standard domain adaptation techniques (low-rank shared branch and high-rank transfer branch) with simple learnable scaling factors, making the core contribution primarily engineering-focused rather than algorithmic

Insufficient analysis of the synthetic-to-real domain gap - while difference maps and t-SNE visualizations are provided, systematic quantitative characterization of what specific texture, material, or lighting properties cause divergence is lacking

Test-time adaptation introduces 0.23 second overhead per image (Table 17), which is non-trivial for real-time applications, with limited discussion of implications or potential computational optimizations

Limited exploration of design choices and alternatives - no comparison with other rendering engines, limited justification for Unreal Engine 5 selection, and insufficient ablation on specific rendering parameter impacts

Motion and dynamic object diversity could be expanded - most examples show person/camera motion with limited exploration of complex multi-object interactions, occlusions, and natural dynamic scene variations
Dataset contributions limited to HDR fusion task - no exploration of generalization to related problems (image denoising, super-resolution, depth estimation), limiting broader impact potential

Incomplete discussion of failure cases and limitations - limited analysis of scenarios where synthetic data doesn't improve performance and which real-world characteristics are well vs. poorly represented
